Pregnancy

X-rays during pregnancy: dose, timing and decisions

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A needed X-ray can help diagnose an injury or illness during pregnancy. An examination performed before you knew you were pregnant does not automatically mean the baby has been harmed. The useful questions are what examination was done, which body area was exposed, the estimated dose reaching the pregnancy and its stage. Most diagnostic examinations use doses well below those associated with developmental harm, but a general reassurance cannot replace assessment of an unusual or substantial exposure.

Start with the reason for the examination

A fracture, dental infection or serious illness may need imaging so that treatment is not delayed. The clinician weighs the consequences of missing the diagnosis against the exposure involved. Pregnancy is a reason to choose and optimize the examination carefully; it is not an automatic reason to refuse necessary imaging.

Tell the referring clinician and radiographer that you are pregnant, might be pregnant or are trying to conceive. Give your estimated pregnancy dates and mention recent related examinations. If an urgent injury or illness is being assessed, tell the team promptly rather than postponing care while you seek an online risk calculation.

The body area matters

A dental, limb, head or chest examination usually keeps the pregnancy outside the direct X-ray beam. Radiation reaching it is much lower than when the abdomen or pelvis is directly examined. The name of the test alone still cannot establish an individual's dose: the technique, number of images, scan coverage and patient characteristics matter.

An abdominal or pelvic examination is not automatically prohibited. It needs a clear clinical reason and a protocol that obtains the necessary information with appropriate exposure. A plain radiograph, a CT scan and a prolonged image-guided procedure can involve very different doses. Do not use the number of appointments as a substitute for the actual examination record.

What rad, gray and milligray mean

Absorbed dose describes energy deposited in tissue. For this discussion, the relevant quantity is the dose reaching the embryo or fetus, usually expressed in milligray, or mGy. One rad equals 10 mGy: 5 rad is 50 mGy and 10 rad is 100 mGy. These conversions do not tell you how much radiation your baby received.

An adult imaging chart may instead show effective dose in millisieverts, or mSv. That is a different measure used to describe overall radiation risk. It cannot simply be substituted for fetal mGy. Likewise, a dose number on a CT report may be a scanner output measure rather than a fetal dose. A radiologist or medical physicist can explain which number you have.

Why 5 or 10 rad is not a personal safety rule

ACOG describes no reported fetal anomalies, growth restriction or pregnancy loss below 50 mGy. UKTIS states that exposure below this level would not usually itself justify termination or extra fetal monitoring. These statements concern particular outcomes and clinical decisions; they do not promise that every possible risk is zero. Most individual diagnostic studies are below this level.

IAEA guidance, drawing on ICRP, says a fetal dose below 100 mGy does not justify termination on radiation grounds alone. This is not permission to aim for that dose, nor does crossing it mean harm is certain or termination is required. Higher or uncertain exposures require specialist assessment of dose, timing and circumstances, with counselling about the available choices.

Pregnancy weeks and developmental timing

Radiation references may count weeks after conception, whereas maternity records usually date pregnancy from the last menstrual period, roughly two weeks earlier. Mixing the two can place an exposure in the wrong developmental period. The first weeks after conception, organ formation and later brain development have different sensitivities at sufficiently high doses.

Statements such as “safe at 3–4 weeks”, “harm above 10 rad at 5–10 weeks” or “brain damage at 11–17 weeks” are too blunt for an individual decision. CDC identifies roughly 8–15 weeks after conception as especially sensitive for intellectual effects from high-dose exposure. Such high-dose observations should not be presented as the expected outcome of a routine dental or limb X-ray.

Later pregnancy is not a no-risk window

At 18–27 weeks of pregnancy, developmental sensitivity differs from earlier pregnancy, but the exposure and the outcome being considered still matter. After 28 weeks, it is misleading to say that the fetus simply has the same risk as the mother. Some developmental effects become less likely later, while a large exposure can still be important.

Cancer risk is a separate question from malformations or effects on brain development. Its size at low diagnostic doses is uncertain, and there is no dependable pregnancy week after which it can be declared absent. This is why neither a gestational-age label nor the absence of a measurable developmental effect proves that an exposure has absolutely no risk.

CT, alternatives and whether to wait

Ultrasound and MRI do not use ionizing X-rays and may answer the clinical question. They are not interchangeable with every radiograph or CT examination, and availability or speed can matter. If they cannot provide the needed information in time, CT may be the appropriate choice. A necessary scan should not be deferred automatically until 20 weeks or after birth.

Ask what the result will change and what could happen if the examination is delayed. The team can decide whether it is genuinely elective or needed now, including after trauma. Contrast material is a separate part of that decision: tell the team about previous contrast reactions and ask why it is required. Iodinated CT contrast crosses the placenta, so its use should have a clinical purpose rather than being treated as identical to a scan without contrast.

Dental imaging and treatment

A painful tooth or dental infection should be assessed during pregnancy. Necessary dental radiographs can be taken at any stage, and delaying urgent treatment can make the problem more complicated. Tell the dentist about the pregnancy and any maternity concerns so that imaging and treatment can be planned together.

Current ADA guidance does not recommend routine abdominal or thyroid shielding for the pregnant dental patient. An absent lead apron therefore does not, by itself, mean unsafe care. Ask the team to explain the indication and its radiation-protection approach; do not avoid needed dental care solely because older advice said every pregnant patient must be shielded.

Why routine patient shielding has changed

A shield on the abdomen does little to block radiation scattered inside the body from the area being examined. If it moves into the image or affects automatic exposure control, it can hide information, lead to another image or increase exposure. AAPM therefore advises against routine patient gonadal and fetal shielding during diagnostic X-ray imaging.

This does not abolish radiation protection. Appropriate examination choice, beam restriction, suitable technique and avoiding unnecessary repeats remain important. Protective barriers and aprons for staff or people assisting during an exposure serve a different purpose. Follow the department's instructions rather than putting a shield in place yourself or assuming every setting uses the same protocol.

If imaging happened before you knew

Contact your maternity clinician and the imaging department with the examination date, body area, type of test and number of examinations. Include any prolonged procedure or radiation treatment, and the best available pregnancy dates. The team can determine whether ordinary reassurance is enough or whether a medical physicist should estimate fetal exposure from the actual records.

An individual calculation is especially useful when substantial abdominal or pelvic exposure is possible, or when several exposures need to be considered together. It is not a sign that damage has already been found. Do not make a pregnancy decision from a generic online dose table. Further monitoring, if indicated, depends on the assessment and any other pregnancy concerns; extra scans are not automatically required after every X-ray.

Before conception and after the examination

Ordinary X-rays and CT do not leave radioactive material in your body. A past diagnostic examination is therefore different from an ongoing source of radiation. Evidence does not support predicting infertility or harm to a future child from an ordinary diagnostic X-ray, but this reassurance should not be extended to high-dose cancer treatment.

If pregnancy may already have begun, disclose that possibility before the examination. Nuclear-medicine tests and radioactive treatments involve different substances and instructions, so ask about the exact procedure rather than using advice about a plain X-ray. Follow any procedure-specific advice about conception; do not invent a universal waiting interval from an online article.

Accompanying a child and working around radiation

You can tell the department that your child needs support and that you are pregnant or might be. Do not hold the child during an X-ray exposure; ask staff to arrange another helper or appropriate support. Follow instructions about where to wait. If you already helped without realizing you were pregnant, report what happened so the department can assess the circumstances rather than assuming the child's dose was also your dose.

If radiation is part of your work, discuss pregnancy with the appropriate supervisor, occupational-health service or radiation safety officer. Review your tasks, monitoring and protective measures under local rules. Continuing work, modifying tasks or changing duties depends on the actual exposure assessment. Patient-dose counselling thresholds are not workplace limits, and advice to stop routine patient shielding does not remove staff protective requirements.

Questions to take to the appointment

Ask: What diagnosis are we checking? Will the result change treatment? Can ultrasound or MRI answer the same question soon enough? What is the risk of waiting? Will the pregnancy be in the direct beam? Does this examination need a fetal-dose estimate? If you were already exposed, ask who will review the records and when you will receive an explanation.

Keep the examination report, dates and the agreed follow-up plan together. If the explanation is unclear or anxiety persists, request a discussion with the radiology or maternity team. Necessary emergency treatment should proceed while the teams coordinate; waiting for a retrospective radiation estimate must not delay assessment of a serious current illness or injury.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Tell the imaging team about pregnancy or its possibility, your dates, and recent relevant examinations before the test.

Ask whether an alternative can answer the question in time and what the consequences of delaying necessary care would be.

For unexpected exposure, keep the actual reports and dates and ask whether radiology or medical-physics review is needed.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps you organize examination dates, reports, pregnancy dates and questions for the maternity and imaging teams. It cannot calculate fetal radiation dose, interpret an image, predict an individual outcome or decide whether you should have a test or continue a pregnancy.

When to seek help

Do not delay assessment of a serious illness or injury because of radiation fears. Tell staff about pregnancy and follow the agreed imaging and treatment plan. Do not calculate fetal risk from adult dose charts, assume a missed apron caused harm, or make a pregnancy decision from a rad threshold alone. Substantial or uncertain exposure requires individualized clinical advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Necessary imaging can protect health during pregnancy; discuss the clinical question and the consequences of delay.
  • Body area, technique, fetal absorbed dose and developmental timing matter more than the label “X-ray”.
  • Neither 5 or 10 rad nor a particular pregnancy week is a universal zero-risk or certain-harm boundary.
  • Routine patient shielding is different from protective measures for workers and helpers.
  • Unexpected exposure should be assessed from actual records, with specialist counselling when needed.

Frequently asked questions

Is an X-ray at 5–10 weeks always dangerous?

No. The body area and actual fetal dose matter, as does whether the weeks are counted from the last period or conception. Early development is sensitive to sufficiently high doses, but this does not make an ordinary dental or limb radiograph equivalent to a high-dose exposure. Ask the imaging team to assess the actual examination.

Does exposure at 11–17 weeks mean brain damage?

No. High-dose research identifies a period of greater brain-development sensitivity, often stated as 8–15 weeks after conception. It cannot predict damage from the pregnancy week alone. A specialist needs the examination details, fetal-dose estimate when indicated and accurate pregnancy dating.

Is imaging risk-free at 18–27 weeks or after 28 weeks?

No pregnancy week is a blanket zero-risk boundary. Developmental sensitivity changes, but dose and type of effect remain important. Later pregnancy should not be described simply as having the mother's radiation risk, and uncertainty about cancer risk is different from the risk of a developmental abnormality.

What determines the risk, and what do 5 and 10 rad mean?

The important factors include fetal absorbed dose, body area, technique, exposure pattern and developmental timing. Five rad equals 50 mGy and 10 rad equals 100 mGy. These are not the same as adult effective-dose figures in mSv, and neither is an automatic safe-or-harmful cutoff for an individual pregnancy.

Should I cancel a necessary CT or dental X-ray?

Discuss the need with the clinical team rather than cancelling because of pregnancy alone. An alternative is useful if it answers the question in time; delaying urgent diagnosis or dental treatment can cause harm. Tell staff about the pregnancy so that they can choose and optimize the examination.

What if I had an X-ray before a positive pregnancy test?

Give your maternity clinician and the imaging department the date, examination and body area. Most diagnostic exposures are reassuring, but substantial or uncertain exposure may need an individual fetal-dose assessment. Diagnostic exposure alone is not an automatic reason to end a pregnancy or arrange extra monitoring.

Does no lead apron mean the baby was unprotected?

No. Routine patient fetal shielding is no longer recommended by major medical-physics guidance, and dental guidance also advises against it. An apron does not stop internal scatter and can interfere with imaging. Staff barriers and protective equipment for people assisting during exposure are a different issue.

Can I hold my child for an X-ray or keep working in radiology?

Do not hold a child during exposure if you are pregnant or might be; tell staff so they can arrange support. Work decisions need an occupational radiation assessment and local precautions, not an automatic ban or a patient-dose threshold. Report any unexpected exposure with its details for advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
